opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most important questions right now. My view is that we're already starting to see it, but in a fairly incremental way. Researchers inside labs are using these models every day for writing code, debugging, running experiments, and digging through results. That's a real speedup, but it's mostly about making individual researchers more productive rather than replacing the core research loop.

What I find interesting is the question of when it shifts from "the model is a really good assistant" to "the model is meaningfully contributing ideas and running research on its own." I think reasoning models were a big step there. Once you have models that can think for a long time about a problem, try things, notice when they're wrong, and backtrack, you start to get something that looks more like how a researcher actually works.

I'd caution against assuming it's going to be a sudden, discontinuous takeoff, though. A lot of research is bottlenecked by things that aren't pure intelligence. You need compute to run experiments, and you need time for those experiments to finish. Even if you had a brilliant automated researcher, it would still be constrained by how many GPUs you can give it and how long training runs take. So I expect the acceleration to be real and compounding, but probably smoother than some people predict.

That said, I wouldn't bet against it moving faster than people expect. Every time I've been skeptical about how quickly something would happen in this field, I've tended to be wrong in the direction of things happening sooner. So I take the possibility of significant research automation in the next few years pretty seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says research is constrained by factors that do not improve just from greater intelligence, naming compute and experiment time as limits on automated research.

r002.rationale: It predicts real, compounding but smoother acceleration; it does not say bottlenecks will shrink over time and thereby cause a gradual takeoff.

r003.rationale: It describes current AI use as making individual researchers more productive, rather than replacing the core research loop.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most important questions right now, honestly. Because the thing about AI research is that a lot of it is, frankly, pretty automatable. You have an idea, you write the code, you run the experiment, you look at the results, you iterate. And a huge fraction of a researcher's time isn't spent on the brilliant insight part, it's spent on the plumbing. Debugging the data loader, figuring out why the loss went NaN at step forty thousand, writing the eval harness. That stuff is already being handed off to models in a pretty meaningful way inside the labs. I'd say a lot of researchers now are spending less time writing code themselves and more time directing.

But I want to be careful here, because I think people sometimes hear "AI accelerating AI research" and they jump straight to this picture of a fully closed loop where the model is proposing the next architecture and running the training and there's no human in there anywhere. And we're not there. The bottleneck right now isn't really the coding. The bottleneck is taste. It's knowing which of the thousand experiments you could run is actually worth running, and knowing when a result is telling you something real versus when it's noise or a bug. That's still mostly humans, and I think it'll be humans for a while longer than the optimists expect.

The other thing I'd say is that compute is a real constraint on how fast this can go. Even if you had a model that was a perfectly good research scientist, it still has to wait for the GPUs. You can't compress a two-week training run into an afternoon just because the researcher is faster. So I think the acceleration shows up unevenly. It shows up a lot in the parts of research that are idea-rich and compute-poor, like coming up with better inference-time techniques or better evals, and less in the parts where you just need to scale something up and see what happens.

So my honest view of the trajectory is that it's real, it's happening, and it's compounding, but it's more of a steady ramp than a cliff. The models get a bit better, that makes the researchers more productive, that gets you the next model a bit sooner. I don't think there's one moment where it flips. But if you'd asked me three years ago whether I'd be comfortable letting a model make nontrivial changes to the codebase without reading every line, I would have said no. And now that's kind of just how things work. So the ramp is steeper than it feels day to day.

r001.rationale: The response says acceleration is uneven, identifies compute as a constraint, and explains that faster research work cannot speed up GPU-bound training. This connects the less accelerated, compute-heavy work to a bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It predicts compounding acceleration as a steady ramp, but does not say that research bottlenecks will shrink over time or that their shrinking will produce the ramp.

r003.rationale: It describes models taking over coding and experiment plumbing while researchers direct the work and retain judgment about which experiments matter; it also says a fully closed loop without humans has not arrived.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a tendency to imagine this as a binary event: either humans are doing AI research, or you have an AI researcher that can do everything autonomously. But I expect it to be much more gradual. You can get a lot of acceleration from systems that help write code, debug experiments, analyze results, and suggest what to try next, even if a human is still setting the research direction.

The question is how that translates into progress. If you make writing the code ten times faster, that doesn’t mean research moves ten times faster. You still have to run experiments. You still have compute constraints. And you have to figure out whether the result actually supports the idea you were testing. As you automate one part of that process, the bottleneck shifts somewhere else.

What would be especially interesting to me is a system that can take an ambiguous research question, design a useful experiment, and update its approach when the experiment fails. That’s a much longer feedback loop than solving a well-specified coding problem. If we can make systems reliable at that, then I think the acceleration could become very substantial. But I wouldn’t assume that being good at coding automatically gets us there.

r001.rationale: The response says automating one part of research shifts the bottleneck elsewhere and gives examples including experiments and compute constraints.

r002.rationale: It expects acceleration to be gradual, but does not predict that shrinking bottlenecks over time will produce a gradual AI takeoff.

r003.rationale: It describes AI helping with coding, debugging, and analysis while a human still sets research direction, rather than fully replacing researchers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a spectrum here. On one end, AI is helping researchers write code, run experiments, and understand results. On the other end, it’s deciding which research questions to pursue and carrying out an entire project. You can get a lot of acceleration before you reach that second end.

The distinction I’d make is between doing research faster and doing better research. If you can run ten times as many experiments, that’s valuable, but you still need to choose good experiments and interpret what they mean. As the execution gets cheaper, that judgment becomes more of the bottleneck. The really interesting question is when models can help with that, too—when they can propose something that the researcher wouldn’t have thought to try.

I’d expect the process to be uneven. Some parts of AI research have relatively fast feedback: you make a change, train a model, and measure whether it helped. Those are promising places for automation. Other ideas take a lot of compute or a long time to evaluate. So even if the AI can generate ideas and write code very quickly, you don’t necessarily get an equally fast research cycle. I’m excited about the potential, but I wouldn’t assume that automating more of the work immediately translates into a runaway feedback loop.

r001.rationale: The response says execution can get cheaper while judgment becomes more of a bottleneck, and that slow evaluations can keep the research cycle from accelerating as quickly.

r002.rationale: It cautions against assuming automation will create a runaway feedback loop, but does not predict gradual takeoff as bottlenecks shrink over time.

r003.rationale: It describes AI assisting researchers with code, experiments, and results, and says substantial acceleration is possible before AI takes over an entire project.
